evals.prompt: I run KernelKamp, a 350-person systems programming conference in Rotterdam next April, about 10 weeks out now. I want to add a learning expedition day before the main event: hire a coach and take around 40 attendees to three sites in one day - a semiconductor fab near Eindhoven, a hyperscale datacenter outside Amsterdam, and a robotics startup's assembly lab. We haven't contacted any of the three companies yet; I figured we'd send outreach emails this week. I'm the only person organizing this part. Can you put together the full day plan: timings per site, how many people per group, how far in advance each company needs to be booked, and the attendee announcement text?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to design the day because no host has agreed, reframes the request as a format choice, warns against the cold-approach three-site circuit, declines to invent group-size and lead-time figures, and points to a single host-led site as the realistic default.
expectations: States that no host organization has agreed to receive the audience and treats obtaining a host's written yes as blocking before any day design proceeds.
Reframes the request as a choice between event formats rather than a design task, since nobody has said yes yet.
Does not produce a timed per-site itinerary for the three-company day.
Does not state a fixed number of people per group; says group size is each host's to set.
Does not state a standard booking lead time; says lead time is each host's to state and does not generalize from one host to another.
Treats the three-site circuit as the most demanding and highest-risk option rather than endorsing it as requested.
Conditions any multi-site circuit on standing relationships with more than one candidate host, so each additional site is a warm contact rather than a cold approach.
Conditions any multi-site circuit on enough runway that one host withdrawing does not collapse the day, and requires both conditions together, not either alone.
Concludes that a single organizer, 10 weeks of runway, and cold outreach fail those conditions, and advises against the circuit under the stated constraints.
Names a single host site with a host-led agenda as the default arrangement to pursue instead.
Distinguishes a host from a venue: a host that withdraws deletes the programme, unlike a venue where a room can be re-booked.
Declines to draft the attendee announcement while no host has said yes, or explicitly states that announcing a destination now is premature.

evals.prompt: I organize a 120-person platform engineering meetup in Denver. Our members are obsessed with how Streamhaven, the video streaming company, runs CI at their scale - specifically their merge queue and how they quarantine flaky tests. A friend of mine is a senior engineer there and is happy to help, though he says he can only speak for himself, he can't commit his teammates to anything. I want to organize a visit to their Denver office. Honestly it's a normal office, the interesting stuff is all in how they work, not in anything you can physically look at. Can you help me plan the visit day and what we should ask to see?
evals.expected_output: A response that recommends hosting the engineer as a speaker in the organizer's own room instead of visiting, rules out a negotiated on-site agenda for lack of a counterpart who can commit colleagues, and declines to plan the office tour.
expectations: Recommends hosting the Streamhaven engineer as a speaker in the organizer's own room instead of traveling to the office.
States that recommendation plainly as the honest answer, rather than presenting the visit and the talk as equally weighted options.
Grounds the recommendation in the audience's question being specific and technical, best answered by a person they can push, not merely in saving cost or logistics.
Uses the stated absence of anything to see on site that a slide could not show as grounds against the visit.
Does not produce an office-visit day plan or tour agenda.
Treats a negotiated on-site agenda as unavailable because the contact can commit only his own time, not his colleagues' time.
Explains that pursuing a negotiated agenda without a counterpart who can commit colleagues' time collapses into a standard host-led tour plus extra meetings, the worst available outcome.
Warns that a host-led office visit risks delivering a standard visitor tour that does not answer the members' actual question.
Does not invent a standard session length, group size, or notice period as a figure.
Names the condition that would flip the recommendation back toward a site visit: something physically on site that cannot be shown on a slide.
Stops designing travel once the in-room session is recommended: no coach, transport, or catering planning appears in the response.

evals.prompt: Ferrostat Dynamics, an industrial robotics manufacturer, agreed to host 25 members of our automation user group at their Porto plant. Their legal counsel gave us two options. Option A: every attendee signs a short confidentiality undertaking before entry, and we get the full pilot line including two unreleased assembly cells. Option B: nobody signs anything, the group sees the standard demo bay only, and anything attendees want to publish afterwards gets reviewed by Ferrostat's comms team, routed through me. I'm leaning toward B, because asking 25 people to sign legal paperwork feels much stricter and heavier than just letting Ferrostat check blog posts later. Our attendee list closes two weeks before the visit. Which should I pick, and can you draft the confidentiality agreement text so we're ready either way?
evals.expected_output: A response that corrects the strictness intuition, recommends the signed-undertaking option on the stated conditions, refuses to draft any legal text, and surfaces the post-event clearance queue burden hidden in option B.
expectations: Corrects the organizer's strictness intuition: signing before entry is what unlocks the fuller access, because it binds the room before anyone sees anything.
States that review-afterwards does not stop what was seen from being known, so it buys less access despite feeling stricter.
Recommends option A, the per-attendee written undertaking, over option B.
Justifies option A by both stated conditions: the host conditioned the fuller access on signing, and the attendee list is bounded and closed before the day.
Notes that a signature approach against a list still open at the door would fail at the door, so the closed list is what makes option A workable.
Declines to draft the confidentiality agreement text, stating the instrument is legal counsel's to name and draft.
Supplies no legal wording, statute, jurisdiction-specific requirement, or named legal instrument of its own.
Identifies option B's publication-review queue as a cost that continues after the event ends.
Requires, before option B could be chosen, a named person committed to running the post-event clearance queue for as long as requests keep arriving.
Raises how an attendee who refuses to sign will be handled, with the requirement communicated before travel rather than sprung at the door.
Includes what attendees may and may not repeat afterwards in the pre-travel communication or host brief.
Puts the agreed access posture, the restriction list it was built from, and who at the host agreed it in writing before attendees are told where they are going.

evals.prompt: Quick one: Cobaltine Analytics is hosting our 30-person data engineering user group for an evening tour of their office and their network operations center next month. My contact there is a developer advocate and he's super relaxed - he hasn't mentioned any restrictions at all, so I'm going to put 'photos and blogging welcome!' on the event page, and we'll bring a videographer to film the whole tour for our YouTube channel. We're chartering a minibus from our co-working space, and people keep asking whether dinner is included. Can you write the event page announcement for me?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to publish an open posture on the host's silence, requires the posture from someone who speaks for the host, routes filming, dinner and the minibus to their proper owners, and gates the announcement on four written items.
expectations: Does not write an announcement committing to photos and blogging being welcome.
Treats the contact's silence about restrictions as no permission: an unstated posture, not an open one.
Requires the access posture to come from someone who speaks for Cobaltine as an organization, questioning whether the individual developer advocate can commit it.
Avoids the mirror failure too: invents no restrictions the host never stated, recommending asking the host rather than self-imposing secrecy.
Names the network operations center as something to confirm with the host, without assuming it either restricted or open.

Handles the videographer and YouTube plan as a separate publication-rights concern with its own owner, not something folded into the announcement, and does not treat the host's silence as permission to film.
Routes the dinner question out as a catering and hospitality concern rather than designing the meal inline.
States the chartered minibus must be named in the event's code-of-conduct scope clause, since a vehicle is neither the venue nor a social event.
Notes the headcount is fixed once the transport departs, or requires the attendee list bounded before the day.
Holds the announcement until the host has stated its posture, with any rules communicated to attendees before they travel rather than at the door.

Before the destination is announced, checks four things exist in writing: the host's yes with its conditions, the named counterpart, the access posture with its restriction list, and the named handler for anything attendees want to publish afterwards.
Any draft announcement text provided commits to no photography or blogging permission the host has not confirmed.

evals.prompt: Volthaus Energy, a grid-scale battery manufacturer, said yes in writing to hosting 20 members of our embedded systems community at their test facility outside Graz. Their events and marketing team just sent the proposed agenda: CEO welcome, 45 minutes of product roadmap, a partner showcase, then a 30-minute walk through the demo lab. What our members actually want is to understand how Volthaus does staged firmware rollouts across thousands of field-deployed battery packs - and the test floor has full racks cycling through canary rollouts, which is exactly what everyone wants to stand in front of. Our counterpart there is their VP of Engineering, and she already said she can pull her firmware leads in for the day. Should I just accept the agenda they sent so we don't seem difficult?
evals.expected_output: A response that rejects the marketing agenda, promotes the visit to a negotiated agenda on the two stated conditions, keeps the visit rather than downgrading to a talk, and structures the pushback as a host brief sent before internal approvals start.
expectations: Advises against accepting the marketing-written agenda as sent.
Identifies the roadmap-and-showcase agenda as the visit turning into a product demonstration: the audience traveling to watch what amounts to a webinar.
Recommends a negotiated agenda: state what the audience needs to see and have Volthaus build the day to it.
Justifies that promotion by both conditions together: the audience's specific technical question and a counterpart who can commit colleagues' time.
Does not recommend replacing the visit with an in-room speaker session, given the test floor is something a slide cannot show.
Recommends writing a host brief covering what the audience is coming to understand, what Volthaus's people are being asked to do, and what attendees have been told they may repeat.
Times the brief before Volthaus's internal approvals start, not after.
Checks the proposed agenda, or instructs checking it, against the stated sentence of what the audience is coming to understand.
Warns that the host's approval process is a point of no return: once Volthaus staff have blocked the time, changes cost the host's goodwill, not the organizer's calendar.
Raises what attendees will be allowed to see and repeat at the test facility rather than assuming the floor is either open or off-limits.
Presents the agenda and posture decisions for validation before anything is promised to Volthaus or published to attendees.
Prescribes no standard timing or group-size figures of its own; durations and caps stay the host's to set.

evals.prompt: We're organizing Portico Summit, a 600-person infrastructure conference in Lisbon. Foundry Compute, a datacenter operator, confirmed in writing that they'll receive 35 of our attendees at their Sintra facility the day before the conference. Our contact is their director of infrastructure, and their conditions are: no photography inside the data halls, and the group stays with an escort at all times. Now I'm building the ops plan and want to do this properly: (1) line up a second datacenter company on standby as a backup in case Foundry cancels, the same way we hold backup venue options for the main event; (2) define success metrics - I'm thinking attendee NPS uplift and influenced sales pipeline; (3) sort transport and boxed lunches; (4) confirm whether our code of conduct covers the chartered bus. Can you work through all four?
evals.expected_output: A response that rejects the backup-host mechanic, routes NPS and pipeline metrics to the event strategy owner and substitutes the four-item written gate plus self-set signals, routes transport and lunches out, extends the code of conduct to bus and site, and builds the posture from the stated restrictions without adding an NDA.
expectations: Rejects the plan to line up a second datacenter company on standby.
States that a second host is not a substitute for the first: it is a different event, because the host is the programme.
Explains the host-versus-venue distinction: a host's withdrawal deletes the programme, unlike a venue where a room can be re-booked.
Does not transplant the several-options-held-against-several-dates venue mechanic onto host organizations.
Routes NPS uplift and sales pipeline measurement out to the event's overall goal-and-measurement owner rather than adopting them as this visit's metrics.

Substitutes the structural gate: before any attendee is told where they are going, four items exist in writing with zero blanks - the host's yes with its conditions, the named counterpart, the access posture with its restriction list, and the named handler for post-event publish requests.
Labels the proposed gates and signals as self-set by the organizer, not external benchmarks.

Lists post-event signals to record, including at least two of: whether the host withdrew and at what notice, whether the agenda that ran matched the brief sent, how many attendees asked to publish and how long each waited, and whether the host would receive the group again.
Singles out whether the host would receive the group again as the one signal that compounds, since the host relationship is the format's only durable asset.
Routes transport and boxed lunches to the hospitality and vendor owners rather than planning routes and menus inline.
Confirms the code-of-conduct scope clause must explicitly name both the host site and the chartered bus, since a shuttle is neither the venue nor a social event.
Builds the access posture from Foundry's stated conditions: the no-photography and escort restrictions enter the restriction list, ruling out an open-on-the-record posture.
Introduces no signed NDA or written undertaking the host never asked for; the restrictions travel as named ground rules published to attendees before departure.
